b: How Scrooge's Redemption Became a Creative, Thematic Adventure

“You will be haunted,” said the Ghost of Jacob Marley, “by Three Spirits.”
“I—I think I’d rather not,” said Scrooge.
Scrooge had absolutely no idea of the adventure that lay in store for him that Christmas Eve. It was the same for me as I set out to turn one of my favorite stories into a playable board game, Spirits of Christmas.
It was the fall of 2021, and I was knee-deep in several other game designs when my daughter Emmie and I began talking about our favorite Christmas movie, Scrooge, starring Albert Finney. As we exchanged favorite quotes from the movie, I commented how fun it would be to have a game in which to actually PLAY Dickens' original tale A Christmas Carol.
I just had to do it. Emmie, who at that time had just been accepted to the University of North Carolina School of the Arts, eagerly accepted the task of illustrating the game. Within a couple of months, I had a strong working prototype, and obtained some volunteer playtesters via BoardGameGeek.

As I typically do for a new game concept, I considered the theme and story of the game, and imagined how I would "play the theme/story." Within a short time, Emmie had her first Scrooge concept in watercolor:
...and I had typed out the first rules set:

This first draft contained the "spirit" of the game mechanisms, but game flow was much more "railroaded", or linear, and offered fewer player choices. Additionally, the prologue section of the game, "London", offered good storytelling but not much actual gameplay value and simply added length to the game.
Therefore, the "London" section was removed, leaving only the three chapters (Past, Present, and Future), which remained the structure of the game until its final form.

Players could now choose from one of four actions each turn: MOVE, PLAY CARDS, DRAW CARDS, or GIVE. While this offered more player choice and deeper strategy, the action system needed one final touch: a rondel mechanism. A rondel would limit the players a bit more, requiring them to plan their actions more carefully.

While a rondel can be quite complex and fascinating, I though it wise to maintain the more relaxed and inclusive "spirit" of a co-op holiday game by keeping the rondel simple and easy to use, while still providing just enough challenge to keep the game crunchy and interesting.

Originally, players would say "Merry Christmas" when giving cards to another player, but this would obviously get old fast as it was not a critical aspect of gameplay. This is where player communication began to work its way in by requiring players to communicate in thematic and cyptic ways, which morphed into sever different communication variants.

Emmie was hard at work creating artwork for the game, using traditional water color to provide classic character and feel. I used her artwork to create a working prototype of the game to share with playtesters.
Our playtesting groups did a phenomenal job of learning the game from the written rules and offering some very helpful ideas. With playtester feedback, some significant changes were made:
• We originally had a cloth bag for the Shilling tokens. We ditched it (too clunky).
• Added Spirit card icons to coin cards, making them more enticing for players.
• Set hand limits for Spirit cards.
• Added the special Spirits cards, one of each type, with its special ability.
• Tweaked the Gift cards to make the powers more balanced.
• Added point icons to the top corners of the point cards for easy stacking.

CROWDFUNDING: ROUND ONE
I had previously run a successful print-and-play campaign, but not one for a printed product. I had a huge learning curve. I did all the research I could, and put in countless days and weeks setting up the campaign and learning about fulfillment options. I ran a modest advertising campaign, and had a small following on the Kickstarter page (in the hundreds). Unfortunately, even though there was sincere interest in the game, the project failed to fund within the first 4 days. I received feedback from my backers (who were very encouraging - they were awesome), and we decided to cancel the project. The main problems were weak timing (April, for a Christmas game), not enough marketing, and the prototype artwork was simply not fulfilling our true vision for the game.
CROWDFUNDING: ROUND TWO
Emmie took a whole new approach to the artwork, creating a similar vibe with all digital artwork, hand drawn by her. She showed me her new samples:

I was ecstatic.
After several months of careful work, Emmie had redrawn nearly every image, capping it off with the final cover art.
I had promised my Kickstarter backers that the project would return, and in December of 2024, it did, running from Thanksgiving to Christmas on Kickstarter. With the new artwork, better marketing, and ideal timing, the campaign was a great success, obtaining the funding necessary to add some great upgrades to the components such as the custom insert (that holds sleeved cards), wooden "meeples" and the Counting House trifold gameboard.

Our Kickstarter backers have been phenomenal. I absolutely must brag on them. This group was supportive, encouraging, and gave fantastic feedback that drove the campaign forward. Even after the campaign was over, the backers' enthusiasm never waned. They stayed with me all the way through to fulfillment, even when some turbulence struck beyond our control. And...we delivered this, our first printed project, to our backers ON TIME! 🎉
I have the backers - and those who supported the game after the campaign - to thank for Spirits of Christmas becoming a reality.
WHAT I LEARNED
Through designing and publishing Spirits of Christmas, I improved my game design process, and learned how to run playtesting, artwork development, marketing, ins and outs of publishing, manufacturing, customs and imports/exports processes, all while maintaining strong customer support and communication with my partners. I think I succeeded overall, and I am a different person because of the journey. What a ride!

I must close with one final thought - one that ties me personally to Spirits of Christmas. I was asked by one the game's reviewers, Matthew Fleming of Meeple Mountain, what I learned from the story of A Christmas Carol. Here is my response:

This story's themes and treatment of morality are rich and deep. Each person will likely take away something different that challenges them. For me, I can empathize with Scrooge as a personality in many ways. There is no time to get into it here, but suffice it to say that my connection to Scrooge has nothing to do with money. His personality type, the way he sees the world, the types of frustration and disappointments he experienced, and how quickly he had forgotten the wonderful things in his past that could have changed his life for the better had he let them.

Scrooge is a warning to not let bitterness and resentment creep into your heart, for it results in distrust of others, leading to lack of concern for others, and that selfishness breeds misery and self-loathing. One excellent passage from the book is spoken to Scrooge by Isabel, his ex-fiance, in the past: “You fear the world too much...All your other hopes have merged into the hope of being beyond the chance of its sordid reproach. I have seen your nobler aspirations fall off one by one, until the master-passion, Gain, engrosses you."
I sincerely hope that more folks will discover Spirits of Christmas and be able to enjoy it this holiday season and many more to come.
I will now end this with a jolly "Merry Christmas" (in or out of season) to you all - and as Tiny Tim said, "God Bless Us, Everyone!"

-John Bailey
Designer and Publisher, Humble Bard Games
